name: Speaking and Pronunciation
title: Speaking and Pronunciation
answer: This idea is that voice tools can give English learners and newcomers more speaking and pronunciation practice than a busy classroom normally allows. It matters because the benefit depends on how the tool is used, with visual support, explicit corrective feedback, peer practice, and level matching. It also matters because young children need teacher judgment, since speech recognition often misreads them.

sections.body: A busy classroom gives each student little time to speak, which makes speaking practice difficult to provide. Voice tools can increase the number of chances a student has to speak. For pronunciation, speech recognition can offer feedback, but it is not automatically effective. The problem it solves is limited oral practice, while the risk it creates is practice that feels active but does not correct the student. The idea therefore pairs the tool with visual support, corrective feedback, peer practice, and teacher oversight.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: With ninth graders, a voice assistant that also shows text and graphics can be used for speaking practice, and the book reports that this worked better than audio alone or practice with teachers and peers. With high school students, pronunciation work should give detailed feedback on specific sounds rather than general feedback. With young children, teachers should rely on their own ears and use speech tools cautiously, because standard speech recognition transfers poorly to children learning English. A school configured voice tool can be set to use simple language with beginners and more complex language as students advance. The teacher sets clear limits on topics and checks in on how students are using it, and the book notes that world language classes in Chapter 9 used similar conversation practice with the same guardrails.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels pronunciation feedback from speech recognition as showing promise with an important caveat. Tai (2022) studied 88 ninth graders and found that a voice assistant with text and graphics led to greater speaking improvement than audio alone or practice with teachers and peers. Ngo et al. (2023) reported a meta analysis with a meaningful average effect, yet most gains appeared when students got explicit corrective feedback and practiced with peers. Bashori et al. (2024) found in a study of 117 high school students that detailed feedback on specific sounds worked better than general feedback, while practice with the tool alone or for a short time showed little benefit. Michot et al. (2024) explain that standard speech recognition is trained mostly on adult native speakers, so it transfers poorly to children learning English and often smooths over their errors instead of catching them.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: For young children, a speech tool may hear what the child intended rather than the actual sounds, so it cannot correct pronunciation. Teachers of young English learners should rely on their own ears and use speech tools cautiously. Pronunciation feedback also needs explicit corrective feedback and peer practice, since practice with the tool alone or for a short time showed little benefit. Conversation practice must match the student's level, with simple language for beginners and more complex language as students advance. The teacher sets clear limits on topics and checks in on how students are using the tool, and those decisions stay with the teacher rather than the tool.
